item.title: GPT 6.1 Sol seems to do worse on long-tail languages.
item.description:
srcreigh wrote in a Hacker News comment:

The ideal language is the one the agent knows how to use.

I used prolog for a project and GPT 6.1 Sol repeatedly made dumb mistakes as if it doesn’t understand the symbolic resolution capabilities.

That made me curious: does Sol do worse when it’s working outside the usual programming languages?

We have some data to look at! We’re working on a battle system for OpenCode, which lets users compare models on their actual tasks. I used Jev to tag the programming languages in all 712 Sol battles, using the requests and available conversation context without showing it the outcomes.

item.title: Get ready for fewer Opus 5.5 em-dashes
item.description:
A few days ago, a popular Hacker News post argued that Opus 5.5 had been nerfed, showing that reasoning tokens declined and language use changed.

In the thread, someone asked if anyone had proof of this, and I realised we did! We are working on a battle system for OpenCode, which gives us data of how Opus 5.5 behaves in comparison to opponents.

Confirming the post

First, we checked if the post is confirmed by our data, and it is! Opus’s reasoning output fell 50.6% relative to matched opponents!

item.title: HN Hiring Index v0.1
item.description:
For a second, let’s pretend Hacker News is a self-contained economy. How is the job market?

We can estimate this using comment counts on the monthly Who is Hiring post for employers and Who Wants to be Hired post for would-be employees.

I built a simple version here: HN Hiring Index v0.1.

Doesn’t this exist?

Yes! HN Hiring Pulse and Santiago Basulto’s analysis.

My only contribution is seasonal adjustment, which the other posts do not include. (What can I say, my introduction to coding was an econometrics class.)

item.title: SlopRouter, or How to Lie with Benchmarks
item.description:
Learning about benchmark saturation - the hard way

It’s 2026, so I built an LLM product that aimed to improve performance. I had a problem, though: how to show that I was actually making an improvement? A benchmark, of course! Unfortunately, no matter how hard I tried, I could not get the benchmark I chose to move. I eventually gave up.

I kept my eye on the leaderboard, though, and noticed strange things start to happen. First, a tiny open weight model nearly matched the frontier for pennies per question. Weird, but maybe AI was advancing that fast. Next, Fable scored worse than Opus.

item.title: About
item.description:
About me

I’m Michael Mayer.

I taught myself to code at night while working as a dishwasher during the day.

I hold an Economics degree and like to read history, memoir, narrative nonfiction and occasionally literature and philosophy.

I worked briefly as a professional developer but always considered myself more of a rapid prototype hacker.

Together with a co-founder, I founded Bottomless, a company that makes automatic re-ordering systems for e-commerce that use weight sensors.
